commenti.body:
I've always thought that the main character is an unreliable narrator. We get all these scenes that seem creepy and weird, because of how they are shot. 

Ben is for sure a weird guy. He definitely sees women as something to conquer. That's why he keeps those little "trinkets of victory". And Ben for sure is a bit weird in the way that he goes around burning greenhouses. But I don't think he's a killer or something.

I think that the main character gets way too attached to the girl and then projects his insecurities on Ben, who seems to be everything that our main character wants to be. We also learn that the girl is quite impulsive and wants to leave this place and move.

The main character just creates this conspiracy in his head and we are supposed to believe it because the film is told from his point of view.

Ben was just a douche who actually considered the main character a friend. Well, friendly enough to share his greenhouse burning shenanigans.

It's interesting how I never realized that whether Ben killed her was open to interpretation. I don't really do too well with films like this. I had simply assumed he did it.

I would love a list of films that are open to the viewers' interpretation, so I can exercise this film-viewing muscle better. But please be gentle, nothing too abstract.

Damn, you're putting me on the spot. It's hard to think of a lot of movies where an event happens and we get a perspective and have to find out if what we saw was true or not.

I guess you can watch more Korean films like Mother or Memories of murder both from Bong, which are both kind of up to interpretation and are also fun thrillers, especially Memories of murder, which is a masterpiece.

The classic, Rashomon from Kurosawa is basically an entire film built around different perspectives regarding an event.

 12 Angry men is a movie set after an event, which we never witness. But the entire movie is a debate about what happened. A really tight drama. This is a favorite of epistemological philosophers.

I guess "The game" and "Inception" are kind of open ended, but I wouldn't count them. They are both fun.

American psycho is a classic that is very open to interpretation. 

American history x is pretty straight forward, but ends kinds open to what will happen next.

​

BUT If you want some generally philosophical movies I can give you a list. My first year of college(I'm studying philosophy) we discussed a lot of movies(one film a week) in order to familiarize ourselves with basic concepts. All pretty straightforward and popular films.

\- Gattaca

\- Truman show

\- The Big Lebowski

\- A serious man

\- Blade runner

\- Dr. Strangelove

\- First reformed

\-  Perfect blue

\- The lives of others

\- Eternal sunshine of a spotless mind

\- Funny games

\- Some random episodes of Always sunny in Philadelphia

\- The matrix

\- I think we had Lars and the real girl, but not sure

I think the debate whether the scenes as shown are “real” vs. imaginative in Jong-Su’s eyes is purposefully unanswerable. It’s way more subtle than American Psycho because in that film the audience is exposed to absolute contradictions and paradoxes (like the apartment lease at the end). I think the Burning film’s creators may have come out and said it’s up to the viewer’s interpretation. 

The insight about Ben’s desire to have a book written about himself and wanting to expose his deeds to Jon-Su can change the way the film is watched next time.
Anatomy of a Fall came out this year and pivots on the central mystery surrounding a woman and if she murdered her husband, and why. It’s riveting and very well-written.
George Romero’s Martin (1977) is fairly ambiguous about whether the lead is really a vampire or just an incredibly abused, mentally ill individual. That one’s pretty open to interpretation.

I’ve just been taking to a colleague about Burning after they recommended it to me and I think this is an interesting theory. I don’t see any ambiguity over the fact that Ben is a/the killer so it’s clear his ego drives him to want to be caught. Perhaps he thinks going along with Jong Su’s meeting means Jong Su might cease to suspect him. I dunno.

Steven Yeun (who plays Ben) said in an interview that the director told him about the character, and he could choose himself whether or not he is a killer. Lee Chang-Dong never knew his interpretation.
